column1: # About This Edition after the light modernising (John, 2026-11-03).

column2: Owen’s text is given as he wrote it — not modernised, abridged, or rewritten. The seventeenth-century spelling stands, save that the long ſ is set as s and words broken across a line are rejoined.
column3: Owen’s text is given as he wrote it in 1668, not abridged or rewritten. The spelling has been brought up to date, so that the book reads easily and sounds rightly when read aloud: wayes is ways, onely is only, perswade is persuade. This edition is lightly modernised, for clear reading and listening, not for interpretation. The old forms are given as we say them now (thou is you, hath is has), references and abbreviations are written out, the capitals that once marked every noun are set as we set them now, and some long sentences are divided by punctuation. A few words whose meaning has changed since 1668 are given in the word we use now, with a lettered note showing the word he wrote; they are listed at the back under Words Brought Forward. Owen’s words, phrases and order of thought are otherwise his own. The British spellings stand, and words broken across a line are rejoined.

column2: • Scripture is left exactly as it was printed, capitals, spelling and all. Those words are not ours to modernise.
column3: • Scripture is quoted as the author quoted it. In a lightly modernised edition its old forms are brought forward with his (thou is you), and nothing else in it is changed.

column2: • The author’s own English is left alone. We may correct his spelling; we do not rewrite him. Thou, hath and doth stand.
column3: • The author’s own English is left alone. We may correct his spelling; we do not rewrite him. A lightly modernised edition brings his old forms forward as well (hath is has), and its About This Edition says exactly what was changed.
